# IPv6 Essentials

IPv6 is not “IPv4 with longer addresses only.” Foundations need **address types**, **prefix notation**, **link-local**, and enough config to run dual-stack labs.

## Learning goals

- Read compressed IPv6 addresses and `/prefix` lengths  
- Distinguish link-local, unique local, global unicast  
- Configure a static IPv6 address on Linux  
- Know what Neighbor Discovery replaces (ARP, parts of ICMP discovery)  

## Why IPv6 in this book

- Dual-stack labs mirror real networks  
- ND and SLAAC appear in operations  
- Many overlays and DC fabrics are IPv6-capable or IPv6-underlay  

You do not need to memorize every transition technology here.

## Address format

- **128 bits**, eight hextets, e.g. `2001:db8:1:2:3:4:5:6`  
- Compress longest zero run with `::` (once)  
- Prefix: `2001:db8:1::/64` (common LAN length is **/64**)  

Documentation prefix: **`2001:db8::/32`** (use in examples).

## Address kinds (must know)

| Kind | Pattern / notes | Role |
|------|-----------------|------|
| **Link-local** | `fe80::/10` | On-link only; required on every interface |
| **Unique local (ULA)** | `fc00::/7` (commonly `fd00::/8`) | Private-like lab space |
| **Global unicast** | `2000::/3` (in practice) | Internet-routable space |
| **Multicast** | `ff00::/8` | One-to-many |
| **Loopback** | `::1` | Local host |
| **Unspecified** | `::` | “Any” / not set |

```bash
ip -6 addr
ip -6 route
```

## Interface identifiers and /64

LAN segments almost always use **/64**. Host bits can come from:

- Manual config  
- SLAAC (router advertisements)  
- DHCPv6 (where used)  

EUI-64 and privacy extensions exist; labs often set **static** addresses for clarity.

## Linux static example

```bash
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:1::10/64 dev eth1
ip link set eth1 up
ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8:1::1 dev eth1
ping -6 2001:db8:1::1
```

## Neighbor Discovery (preview)

IPv6 uses **ND** (ICMPv6) instead of ARP:

- Neighbor Solicitation / Advertisement  
- Router Solicitation / Advertisement  

Details: [ARP, ND, and Local Resolution](07-arp-nd-and-local-resolution.qmd).

## Dual-stack thinking

| Stack | Failure isolation |
|-------|-------------------|
| IPv4 works, IPv6 fails | v6 route, RA, ND, firewall ip6tables/nft |
| Prefer AAAA vs A | Happy Eyeballs / app order |

Test **both** when dual-stack is in scope:

```bash
ping -4 <host>
ping -6 <host>
```

## Address scope and choosing a next hop

IPv6 is not simply IPv4 with longer addresses. A link-local address (`fe80::/10`) is valid only on its link and is often used as a router's next hop. The same link-local address can exist on different interfaces, so a host may need an interface or zone identifier such as `fe80::1%eth1`. A global unicast address can be routed beyond the link subject to policy. Unique local addresses are intended for local communication, but their existence does not itself prevent a route or filter from leaking them.

A host learns on-link prefixes, default routers, and other parameters from router advertisements according to their flags and lifetimes. SLAAC and DHCPv6 are separate mechanisms: receiving an address is not the same as receiving a default route, and DHCPv6 does not normally provide the default router. Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6, including Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, instead of ARP. IPv6 uses multicast rather than IPv4-style broadcast.

The IPv6 base header has a Hop Limit, reduced by forwarding routers. Routers do not fragment IPv6 packets; they report Packet Too Big when an outgoing link cannot carry a packet. Do not block ICMPv6 indiscriminately: Neighbor Discovery and path-MTU feedback depend on it. Inspect `ip -6 addr`, `ip -6 route`, and `ip -6 neigh` together to distinguish address, route, and neighbor failures. See [RFC 8200](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200.html).


## Checkpoint

Write a dual-stack plan for one LAN: IPv4 `/24`, IPv6 `/64` from `2001:db8:10::/64`, gateway `::1` / `.1`, two hosts.
